title: JobRepository Purpose and Schema
summary: The JobRepository is not an optional audit log — it is the central nervous system of Spring Batch. Every restart, every skip, every commit boundary, and every flow decision depends on the data stored in its tables. Without the JobRepository, Spring Batch is just a fancy for loop. With it, the framework becomes a stateful, recoverable, observable execution engine. Understanding what the tables store and how they relate to the domain model (Section 2) is essential for debugging production failures, tuning performance, and designing restart-safe jobs.

The schema consists of six core tables. BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE stores the logical identity of a job run: the job name plus the JobParameters that uniquely identify it. Identical parameters for the same job name always resolve to the same JOB_INSTANCE_ID. This is why rerunning with identical parameters throws JobInstanceAlreadyCompleteException (see 2.1) — the framework looks up this table and finds the instance already exists with a completed execution. BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION stores each physical attempt to run a JobInstance: start time, end time, status (STARTED, COMPLETED, FAILED), and exit code. A failed job that is restarted creates a new row here, linked to the same instance. BATCH_JOB_PARAMS stores the key-value pairs of JobParameters as typed columns (STRING_VAL, LONG_VAL, DATE_VAL, etc.) linked to the instance.

BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION is where the operational action lives. Every step in every job execution gets a row here, tracking read_count, write_count, commit_count, rollback_count, skip_count, and timing. When you partition a step (Section 11), each partition produces its own STEP_EXECUTION_ID row, all linked to the same parent JOB_EXECUTION_ID. This is why a single partitioned job can write 50 or 100 rows to this table. The STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXT and JOB_EXECUTION_CONTEXT tables store the serialized ExecutionContext objects (see 2.3) as BLOBs or CLOBs. These are the restart bookmarks: the line number in a CSV file, the last-read primary key in a database cursor, the cumulative mismatch count across steps. When a job restarts, the framework deserializes these contexts and hands them back to the readers and listeners so execution resumes exactly where it left off.

The schema is designed for append-only, immutable history. Rows are never updated to change a past status; instead, new executions are created. This makes the JobRepository a complete audit trail. In financial reconciliation, regulators may ask for proof that a job ran on a specific date, how many records were processed, and whether any were skipped. The BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION table answers all of these questions without custom logging. However, this append-only design means the tables grow indefinitely. Production deployments must implement an archiving or purging strategy (typically via Spring Batch's JobRepository metadata cleanup APIs or direct SQL) to prevent the tables from consuming unbounded storage. A common pattern is to purge executions older than 90 days, retaining only the most recent successful execution per JobInstance for restart purposes.
keyPoints: The JobRepository is the stateful execution engine of Spring Batch — not just an audit log.
BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE stores the logical identity (job name + parameters); identical parameters always resolve to the same instance.
BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION stores each physical attempt; restarts create new rows linked to the same instance.
BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION tracks per-step metrics (read/write/commit/skip counts) and timing.
JOB_EXECUTION_CONTEXT and STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXT store serialized restart bookmarks.
The schema is append-only; production deployments need archiving/purging strategies to prevent unbounded growth.

note.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
note.text: When a job fails at 3 AM, your first diagnostic step is querying BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION for the failed step's status, commit count, and exception message. Understanding the schema turns a panic into a 30-second SQL query.

quiz.question: A job named reconciliationJob with parameters {processDate=2026-07-15} failed on its first run. An operator restarted it, and it completed successfully on the second attempt. How many rows exist in BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION for this JobInstance after the restart?

options.label: 1 — the failed execution is overwritten with the successful status
2 — one row for the initial failed attempt and one row for the successful restart
3 — one for the initial run, one for the restart, and one for the final completion summary
0 — the JobRepository only stores the most recent execution per instance

quiz.explanation: The JobRepository schema is append-only. A failed execution creates a BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION row with status FAILED. A restart creates a new JobExecution row linked to the same JobInstance, with its own STARTED/COMPLETED/FAILED status. The failed row is never deleted or overwritten. This immutable history is essential for audit trails and debugging. Two rows total: one FAILED, one COMPLETED.

title: JdbcJobRepository Setup
summary: Spring Batch 5.2 requires a real relational database for the JobRepository. The in-memory map-based repository was removed in 5.x (see 3.5), so even local development needs a real database — typically H2, PostgreSQL, or an embedded database. The JdbcJobRepository is the standard implementation, and it stores all execution metadata in the six tables described in 3.1. Setting it up correctly is not just about getting the tables created; it is about configuring isolation levels, table prefixes, and schema initialization so that the repository behaves correctly under concurrent access and restart scenarios.

The JobRepository is created automatically by Spring Boot 3.5 auto-configuration if it detects Spring Batch on the classpath and a DataSource bean. The auto-configuration uses the primary DataSource by default. You can customize this by providing a dedicated DataSource for the JobRepository — useful when you want to isolate metadata contention from business transactions (see 11.14). The key property is spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema, which controls whether Spring Boot creates the batch tables on startup. Values are always (create every time, useful for H2 in tests), embedded (create only for embedded databases like H2, the default), and never (assume a DBA has created the tables, required for production databases where the application should not have DDL privileges).

The default transaction isolation level for JobRepository operations is ISOLATION_SERIALIZABLE. This is the strictest level: it prevents phantom reads, which is critical because the framework queries BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE to check if a job already exists with the same parameters, then inserts a new BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION row. If two threads launch the same job with identical parameters simultaneously, serializable isolation prevents both from creating duplicate executions. However, SERIALIZABLE is expensive on some databases (notably Oracle and SQL Server) and can cause lock contention or serialization failures under high concurrency. You can override this via BatchConfigurer or by customizing the JobRepositoryFactoryBean to use ISOLATION_REPEATABLE_READ or ISOLATION_READ_COMMITTED if your database and concurrency patterns allow it. For most reconciliation jobs with single-threaded or moderately concurrent launches, the default is safe.

The tablePrefix property allows multiple Spring Batch applications to share the same database schema without table name collisions. By default, the prefix is BATCH_, producing table names like BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION. If you set tablePrefix=RECON_, the tables become RECON_JOB_EXECUTION, etc. This is useful in environments where a single database instance hosts multiple batch applications and the DBA prefers namespace separation over separate schemas. When changing the prefix, you must also ensure the schema initialization scripts (if used) create tables with the matching prefix. Spring Boot does not auto-adjust the DDL scripts for custom prefixes; you must provide your own schema-*.sql files or use a database migration tool like Flyway or Liquibase.
keyPoints: Spring Boot 3.5 auto-configures the JdbcJobRepository using the primary DataSource.
spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema controls DDL: always (dev/test), embedded (default), never (production).
Default isolation is SERIALIZABLE to prevent duplicate job executions under concurrent launches; override if your database struggles with it.
tablePrefix allows multiple applications to share one database; requires matching DDL scripts.
For production, use never and manage schema via Flyway/Liquibase with application-specific migration files.

note.label: WARNING
note.text: Never set spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=always in production. If the application restarts, it will attempt to recreate existing tables, which fails or drops data depending on the script. Use 'never' in production and manage schema via your migration tool.

quiz.question: Your production PostgreSQL database hosts two Spring Batch applications: reconciliation-service and settlement-service. Both use the default BATCH_ table prefix. What is the most likely operational problem?

options.label: PostgreSQL cannot handle two applications writing to the same schema simultaneously
The two applications will collide on the same table names, causing one app to see the other's job executions and potentially corrupt metadata
Spring Batch automatically creates separate schemas for each application
The JobRepository uses row-level locking that prevents concurrent access across applications

quiz.explanation: With the default BATCH_ prefix, both applications write to the same tables (BATCH_JOB_INSTANCE, BATCH_JOB_EXECUTION, etc.). Application A's job executions are visible to Application B's JobExplorer queries. Worse, if both apps have a job named 'nightlyJob', they will share the same JobInstance rows because the instance key is (jobName + parameters). This causes cross-application corruption, restart failures, and incorrect dashboard metrics. The fix is to use distinct table prefixes (e.g., RECON_ and SETTLE_) or separate database schemas.

title: @EnableBatchProcessing — Version-Critical
summary: In Spring Boot 2.x and early Spring Batch 4.x, @EnableBatchProcessing was the standard way to activate Spring Batch auto-configuration. It triggered the creation of a JobRepository, JobLauncher, JobExplorer, and JobOperator from the application's DataSource and transaction manager. In Spring Boot 3.5 with Spring Batch 5.2, this annotation has a subtle but critical behavior change: adding it disables Spring Boot's auto-configuration for batch infrastructure. Instead, the annotation's own configuration takes over, creating beans based on the annotation's attributes rather than Boot's properties.

This means that in Boot 3.5, if you add @EnableBatchProcessing to your main application class without any customization, you are actively turning off the smarter auto-configuration that reads spring.batch.* properties from your application.yml. Properties like spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema, spring.batch.job.names, and spring.batch.jdbc.schema may be ignored because the annotation-based configuration does not know about them. The beans created by the annotation use default settings: the primary DataSource, a default table prefix, and no schema initialization. This is a common source of confusion when developers migrate from Boot 2.x: they add the annotation out of habit, and suddenly their spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=never property is ignored, causing table creation failures in production.

The correct rule for Spring Boot 3.5 is: do not add @EnableBatchProcessing unless you are explicitly customizing the JobRepository or PlatformTransactionManager in ways that Boot's auto-configuration cannot handle. If you need a custom JobRepository (e.g., with a non-default DataSource, a custom table prefix, or a different isolation level), you should define the JobRepository bean explicitly in a @Configuration class (see 3.2) and let Boot auto-configure everything else. If you need a custom PlatformTransactionManager for batch (e.g., a JTA transaction manager spanning multiple resources), define that bean and let Boot wire it into the auto-configured JobRepository. Only if you need to override multiple infrastructure beans in a coordinated way should you consider @EnableBatchProcessing — and even then, you are opting out of Boot's property-driven configuration.

The annotation also has a modular attribute (@EnableBatchProcessing(modular = true)) that was used in Spring Batch 4.x to support dynamic job registration from multiple modules. In Spring Batch 5.2, this attribute is deprecated and has no effect. In Spring Batch 6.0, the entire @EnableBatchProcessing annotation is deprecated in favor of a new BatchConfigurer interface and explicit bean configuration. If you are writing code today that will migrate to 6.0, prefer explicit bean configuration over the annotation. This lecture's code shows the Boot 3.5 / Batch 5.2 pattern: no annotation, explicit beans only when needed, and full reliance on auto-configuration for the standard case.
keyPoints: In Spring Boot 3.5, @EnableBatchProcessing disables Boot's batch auto-configuration.
Without the annotation, Boot auto-configures JobRepository, JobLauncher, and JobExplorer from spring.batch.* properties.
Only add the annotation if you need explicit, coordinated customization of multiple infrastructure beans.
For custom JobRepository or transaction manager, define the bean explicitly and let Boot auto-configure the rest.
modular = true is deprecated in 5.2 and removed in 6.0; prefer explicit configuration for future-proofing.

note.label: DECISION POINT
note.text: If you add @EnableBatchProcessing out of habit from older Spring Boot versions, you will silently lose all spring.batch.* property configuration. Remove it unless you have a specific, documented reason to override the auto-configuration.

quiz.question: A developer migrating from Spring Boot 2.7 to Spring Boot 3.5 keeps @EnableBatchProcessing on the main application class. They set spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=never in application.yml, but the application still attempts to create batch tables on startup. What is the root cause?

options.label: The property name changed in Spring Boot 3.5 and should be spring.batch.schema.initialize
@EnableBatchProcessing disables Boot's auto-configuration, so the property is ignored and the annotation's default behavior (initialize schema) takes over
The application.yml file is not being loaded because the profile is not active
Spring Batch 5.2 no longer supports the never option for schema initialization

quiz.explanation: In Spring Boot 3.5, @EnableBatchProcessing opts out of Boot's batch auto-configuration entirely. The annotation-based configuration does not read spring.batch.* properties. It uses its own defaults, which include schema initialization behavior that may differ from Boot's auto-config. Removing the annotation restores Boot's property-driven auto-configuration, respecting spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=never. The property name did not change, and never is still a valid value.

title: JobBuilder and StepBuilder Fluent API
summary: In Spring Batch 5.x, the factory-based configuration pattern (JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory) was removed. These factories were convenient in Spring Batch 4.x because they automatically injected the JobRepository into every builder, but they created tight coupling between job configuration classes and the framework's internal factory infrastructure. In Spring Batch 5.2, the builder classes (JobBuilder and StepBuilder) are instantiated directly via their constructors, and the JobRepository (and PlatformTransactionManager for steps) is passed explicitly. This change is not just cosmetic — it makes the dependencies visible, testable, and compatible with Spring Boot 3.5's constructor-based auto-wiring.

The JobBuilder constructor takes two arguments: the job name (a String) and the JobRepository. The job name is used to identify the job in the JobRepository and must be unique within the application. The JobRepository is where the job's execution metadata is stored. From the JobBuilder, you chain methods to define the job's flow: .start(Step) for a single-step job, or .start(Step).on(ExitStatus).to(Step).from(...) for conditional flows (see Section 12). The builder returns a Job bean that Spring manages and that the JobLauncher can execute. Because the JobRepository is injected via constructor, you can write pure unit tests for your job configuration by passing a mock or in-memory repository — though remember, there is no true in-memory repository in 5.x (see 3.5).

The StepBuilder constructor also takes the step name and the JobRepository. For chunk-oriented steps, you then call .<InputType, OutputType>chunk(chunkSize, transactionManager) to specify the chunk size and the PlatformTransactionManager that will manage the chunk transactions. This generic type declaration (<TransactionRecord, ReconciledTransaction>) is what allows the compiler to enforce that the reader produces TransactionRecord, the processor accepts TransactionRecord and produces ReconciledTransaction, and the writer accepts ReconciledTransaction. If the types do not align, the compilation fails — a type safety improvement over the raw-type factories in 4.x. After the chunk declaration, you chain .reader(), .processor(), and .writer() to wire the components.

For tasklet steps (see 4.3), the builder pattern is similar but uses .tasklet(Tasklet, transactionManager) instead of .chunk(). The Tasklet interface and the transaction manager are passed directly. The fluent API supports additional configuration methods that are shared across step types: .listener() to add execution listeners (Section 8), .faultTolerant() to enable skip/retry (Section 9), .taskExecutor() to add multi-threading (Section 11.2), and .startLimit() to restrict how many times a step can be started. These methods are available on the builder returned by .chunk() or .tasklet(), so the configuration flows naturally from the step type declaration to its behavioral tuning. The key mental model: the builder is a declarative configuration object, not an imperative script. It describes what the step should do; the framework executes it later.
keyPoints: JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory were removed in Spring Batch 5.x.
JobBuilder and StepBuilder are instantiated directly with JobRepository passed explicitly.
Chunk steps use .<I, O>chunk(size, transactionManager) for type-safe reader/processor/writer wiring.
Tasklet steps use .tasklet(tasklet, transactionManager).
The fluent API supports .listener(), .faultTolerant(), .taskExecutor(), and .startLimit() chaining.
Constructor injection of JobRepository makes configuration testable and aligned with Spring Boot 3.5 patterns.

note.label: KEY INSIGHT
note.text: The explicit constructor pattern makes your job configuration a plain Spring bean with visible dependencies. This is not just cleaner — it is the only pattern that survives into Spring Batch 6.0 without deprecation warnings.

quiz.question: A developer migrating from Spring Batch 4.x writes the following configuration. What is wrong with it for Spring Batch 5.2 / Spring Boot 3.5? @Autowired private JobBuilderFactory jobBuilderFactory; @Autowired private StepBuilderFactory stepBuilderFactory;

options.label: The factories still exist but are deprecated; the code compiles with warnings
The factories were removed in Spring Batch 5.x; the code will not compile
The factories work but disable Spring Boot 3.5 auto-configuration
The factories require @EnableBatchProcessing to be present, which is no longer recommended

quiz.explanation: JobBuilderFactory and StepBuilderFactory were removed entirely in Spring Batch 5.x. They do not exist in the classpath. Any code referencing them will fail to compile. The replacement is direct constructor injection of JobRepository and explicit instantiation of JobBuilder and StepBuilder. Option D is a distractor: while @EnableBatchProcessing is no longer recommended, the factories themselves are gone regardless of the annotation.

title: Why There's No In-Memory Repository Anymore
summary: In Spring Batch 4.x and earlier, a MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean provided an in-memory, non-persistent JobRepository backed by a ConcurrentHashMap. It was convenient for unit tests and quick demos: no database setup, no schema scripts, no connection pools. You could run a batch job in a test and it would execute in memory, leaving no trace. In Spring Batch 5.x, this was removed entirely. The rationale was not arbitrary — it was a deliberate design decision to enforce production-grade behavior from the first line of code. The in-memory repository created a dangerous illusion: jobs appeared to work in tests but would fail in production because the real JdbcJobRepository has different transactional behavior, serialization constraints, and performance characteristics.

The practical implication is that even local development and unit tests need a real database. The standard approach in Spring Boot 3.5 is to use an embedded database like H2 for tests and local development, and a real database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle) for production. H2 is lightweight, starts in-process, and Spring Boot auto-configures it with spring.batch.jdbc.initialize-schema=embedded (the default), which creates the batch tables automatically. This gives you the convenience of 'no setup' while still using the real JdbcJobRepository code path. Your tests exercise the same repository implementation that runs in production, eliminating the 'works on my machine' class of bugs where in-memory behavior diverges from JDBC behavior.

The removal also forces developers to think about schema initialization and migration from day one. With the in-memory repository, schema was irrelevant — there was no schema. With H2 or PostgreSQL, you must decide how tables are created: Boot auto-initialization for dev/test, Flyway or Liquibase migrations for production. This friction is intentional. It ensures that when the application reaches production, the team has already solved the schema management problem, tested it in staging, and documented the migration scripts. The alternative — discovering on production deployment day that the application tries to create tables it does not have privileges for — is a common failure mode that the removal of the in-memory repository prevents.

For integration tests, the pattern is to use @SpringBootTest with an H2 in-memory database (configured via application-test.yml) and let Boot auto-create the batch schema. For end-to-end job tests, JobLauncherTestUtils (see 14.1) launches the job against this real H2 repository, and you can query the results using JobExplorer or direct JDBC queries. The test validates not just business logic but also restart behavior, ExecutionContext persistence, and transaction commit/rollback — all of which were silently skipped with the old in-memory repository. The cost is a slightly slower test startup (H2 initialization takes ~1 second), but the confidence gained is worth it for any job that will run in production.
keyPoints: MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean was removed in Spring Batch 5.x to enforce production-grade behavior in all environments.
Even local development and tests must use a real database (H2 for dev/test, PostgreSQL/MySQL/Oracle for production).
H2 with initialize-schema=embedded provides 'zero setup' convenience while using the real JdbcJobRepository code path.
The removal forces teams to solve schema management (Flyway/Liquibase) before production deployment.
Integration tests with H2 validate restartability, ExecutionContext persistence, and transaction behavior — all skipped by the old in-memory repository.

note.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
note.text: The in-memory repository hid transaction and serialization bugs that only appeared in production. Using H2 in tests means your first encounter with a JDBC serialization exception or isolation-level deadlock happens in a test, not at 2 AM on a production database.

quiz.question: A team migrating from Spring Batch 4.x to 5.2 discovers that their extensive unit test suite, which relied on MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean, no longer compiles. They argue that H2 is unnecessary overhead for 'simple' tests. What is the strongest technical counter-argument?

options.label: H2 is faster than the old Map-based repository for large datasets
The Map-based repository had memory leaks that H2 avoids
Tests against the Map-based repository did not exercise JDBC serialization, transaction boundaries, or isolation levels, allowing bugs to reach production undetected
Spring Boot 3.5 does not support H2 and requires PostgreSQL even in tests

quiz.explanation: The primary rationale for removing MapJobRepositoryFactoryBean was that it created a false sense of security. Code that passed tests against the in-memory repository could fail in production due to JDBC-specific behavior: serialization of ExecutionContext (which catches non-serializable objects), transaction isolation level effects (e.g., SERIALIZABLE deadlocks), and connection pool exhaustion. H2 uses the exact same JdbcJobRepository code path as PostgreSQL, so these issues are caught in tests. Speed (option A) and memory leaks (option B) are not the primary concerns. Spring Boot 3.5 absolutely supports H2 (option D is false).
